campaign.summary: Anthropic's loop has no classic algorithms round. Prep time therefore goes only to practical coding (about 75%, matching its 0.48 combined round weight) and system design (about 25%). Weeks 1-3 cover the most-asked stateful 4-level OA builds and the design prerequisites (KV store, caching, rate limiting) before the inference-flavored designs. The middle weeks drill extensions (thread safety, persistence, TTL) as timed reviews, and the final week is pure consolidation with timed reruns of the highest-weight problems.

advice: Practice timed 90-minute, 4-level simulators (in-memory KV DB with TTL and scans, bank with transaction log, task manager with dependencies) in Python with only the standard library. Minimize bugs, since every test at a level must pass to move on.

Master the web crawler end to end: BFS restricted to the same host, then thread-pool or async workers with a thread-safe visited set and clean termination. Don't announce that you've memorized it; that has led to an extra round and a downlevel.

For any cache or store problem, expect follow-ups on thread safety, error handling and persistence or crash recovery (e.g. a write-ahead log). Keep the code running at each step rather than over-engineering serialization.

Prepare a real 'Why Anthropic', read the culture documents the recruiter sends, and be ready to give an honest critique of Anthropic's direction and to reason through ethical dilemmas several follow-ups deep.
For system design, treat LLM prompts as classic infra: batching up to the GPU limit, queues, routing, backpressure and overload, observability. Narrate trade-offs collaboratively.
company.interview_format: Anthropic runs one generalist SWE loop. Public reports are rarely labeled mid-level, so level-specific details are low confidence. The usual sequence is a recruiter screen, then a 90-minute CodeSignal 'Industry Coding Assessment' (one stateful system built up over 4 levels, usually in Python), sometimes followed by a ~60-minute live practical coding screen, then a hiring manager screen. The virtual onsite on Google Meet has 4–5 rounds of about 55 minutes: practical coding, system design (often infra/inference flavored), project deep dive, a culture/values round with deep ethical follow-ups, and a hiring manager behavioral round. Coding is practical rather than classic LeetCode and checks fast, correct, extensible code, concurrency and persistence; team matching happens after the onsite.

topic_weights.why: The OA, phone screen and onsite coding are all practical: stateful systems, crawler concurrency, LRU with persistence.
GPU inference batching is the most reported design prompt; also token generation at 100k RPS and model distribution.
The web crawler (BFS/DFS plus concurrency) is the most reported coding question; the task manager OA uses dependency/topological ordering.
Hash maps underpin the KV database, bank, file dedup (LC 609) and LRU key generation.
File cache system, key-value store and distributed search prompts are reported.
Batching queues, messaging at 100M DAU, telemetry pipelines.
LRU cache (hashmap plus doubly linked list) is a reported phone-screen question.
The profiler / function-event problem and Exclusive Time of Functions in the dataset use call-stack processing.
Chat app / Claude chat service, prompt playground, developer APIs.
Overload behavior, backpressure, observability are probed in design and hiring manager rounds.
Time-based KV lookups with TTL or timestamps loosely map to LC 981; moderate, thin evidence.
Distributed mode/median (infra) and scheduling extensions; thin evidence.
Event start/end processing appears in the profiler-style questions; thin evidence.
No reports of DP; Anthropic is described as 'not leetcode'.

scores.note: The candidate quickly set concrete targets (100k reads/s, 20k writes/s, p99 under 10ms, 10TB, 1MB values, read-your-writes for some clients), but skipped the interviewer's direct question about whether writes should succeed or be rejected during a network partition.

The API was only put/get/delete with size limits, with no versioning or timestamps on values, no per-request consistency option, and no conditional writes, even though some clients need read-your-writes.

The design covered a stateless router with consistent hashing and virtual nodes, 3x cross-zone replication with a leader, a WAL, LSM storage, and heartbeat-based failover, but it mixed in hinted handoff, a mechanism from leaderless Dynamo-style designs, without explaining how it fits a leader-based model.

There was no capacity math (10TB x3 replicas → node count), and nothing on hot keys, rebalancing when nodes join, compaction's effect on the 10ms p99, or the durability gap the interviewer was probing about when writes are acknowledged.

The candidate answered the CAP partition question with an architecture dump instead, so the interviewer had to say 'You skipped my partition question' and rephrase it around write acknowledgment and failover, and the session ended without that trade-off being addressed.

strengths: Concrete, well-quantified functional and non-functional requirements up front
Sensible partitioning choice (consistent hashing with virtual nodes)
Storage engine choice (WAL + LSM) justified implicitly by write-heavy load
Cross-zone replication and an explicit failure-handling story (membership service, leader promotion)
scorecard.summary: You set strong, quantified requirements and sketched a credible leader-based architecture with consistent hashing, cross-zone replication, and an LSM engine well matched to your workload. However, you sidestepped the core consistency question (what happens to writes during a partition or right after a failover), and the interviewer had to redirect you, so quorum consistency and conflict resolution were never covered.
weak_concepts: CAP behavior under network partition: rejecting writes (CP) vs accepting them (AP), and stating the choice explicitly
Synchronous vs asynchronous replication acks and their durability/latency cost
Losing acknowledged writes when an async-replicated leader fails over
Quorum reads/writes (R + W > N) as a tunable consistency mechanism
Conflict resolution and versioning (vector clocks, last-write-wins, sibling values)
Split-brain prevention during leader election (epochs/terms, fencing tokens)
Hinted handoff in leaderless vs leader-based replication
Hot-key mitigation and rebalancing when nodes join or leave
